generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology uses the language of criticality precisely. To analyse a study is to separate its claim, its method and its evidence; to evaluate it is to weigh how well the method supports the claim; to synthesise is to draw several studies into a position of your own; to judge is to say, with reasons, what the evidence will bear. Assignment briefs in psychology use these words as instructions, and knowing what each asks is how you give a marker what they want.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are asked to write about the same study for a seminar.

Tom writes: the study found a large effect, and the authors concluded it was important. This is accurate, and it is a description: it reports what the study says but adds nothing of Tom's own.

Amara writes: the study reports a large effect, but the sample was small and drawn from one population, so its claim to importance is not yet secure. This is a judgement: it still reports the study, but it weighs the evidence and reaches a reasoned position.

Both understood the study. Only Amara moved from describing it to judging it, the step the language of criticality names.
generatedProse.summary: Psychology's working vocabulary, analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement, names the moves of critical thinking. You can now use these words correctly, tell a judgement apart from a description, and name the move a psychology brief is asking for. With the mindset, the active habits and the language in place, you are ready to be critical on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's sentence a judgement rather than a description?

items.text: It weighed the evidence (a small, unrepresentative sample) and reached a reasoned position.
It reported the study's findings more accurately than Tom's.
It was longer than Tom's sentence.
It quoted the authors' own conclusion.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the evidence and taking a reasoned position is what makes it a judgement.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the sentence did beyond reporting: weighing and taking a position.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's sentence was a judgement because it weighed the sample and reached a reasoned position. Accurate reporting, length or a quotation are all still description.
